name: trilogy-component-architecture
description: "Analyze or apply Trilogy component architecture, atomic composition, and separation of UI and functional props for Figma-to-React and React-to-Figma workflows."

# Trilogy Component Architecture and Composition

## Analysis and compatibility

1. Read the repository instructions, then inspect the component, subcomponents, types, exports, stories, tests, Web and Native implementations, and comparable components. Preserve existing local changes. For an existing component, determine its actual contract, defaults, and platform differences; do not infer behavior from names alone.
2. Distinguish UI props and their visual values/states from functional props such as events, navigation, business logic, semantics, accessibility, refs, and children. Do not remove, reset, or change existing behavior or functional props; do not blindly pass UI props through to the DOM or React Native.
3. If design and code conflict, use the source of truth appropriate to the requested direction: verified Figma for Figma-to-React, existing code for React-to-Figma. Report differences and ask before incompatible, functional, or otherwise unrequested changes. Do not automatically remove an existing UI prop absent from the design without explicit authorization.
4. Do not directly edit files marked as generated until their generator and source are identified. If no usable generator exists, report the blocker and ask how to proceed.

## Structure and composition

- Follow the organization used in `packages/react/src/components`: one folder per component, a consistent public `index.ts` barrel, `<name>.types.ts`, separate `*UiProps` and `*Props`, `<name>.web.tsx` and `<name>.native.tsx` implementations, `<name>.styles.native.ts` using `makeStyle` for theme-dependent styles, and `<name>.stories.tsx`. Follow actual repository conventions and omit platform suffixes in barrel imports; do not add empty files.
- **Every component and every public subcomponent has its own folder containing its own `<name>.types.ts` and `index.ts`.** The subcomponent's props interface, enums and value types are declared in that file (for example `alert/alert.types.ts` and `alert/content/alertContent.types.ts`), and its `index.ts` exports the component and `export * from "./<name>.types"`. The parent's `index.ts` only exports the parent and re-exports each subcomponent folder (`export * from "./content"`). Never declare a subcomponent's props or types in the parent's `.types.ts`, in a family-wide types file at the component root, or in any file shared by all subcomponents. When sibling subcomponents accept the same prop, declare it in each of their own types files rather than in a shared root interface. Only a type that is genuinely cross-cutting (for example a value the parent shares with its children) lives in the parent's `.types.ts`, and subcomponents import it from there. Before finishing, verify that every `*.types.ts` sits next to the one component it describes, as `Alert` and `Accordion` do.
- **A prop with several possible values (size, appearance, status, position, orientation, ...) is typed with a string `enum`, never with a standalone `type X = "a" | "b"` or an inline union of string literals.** Declare the enum in the component's own `<name>.types.ts`, named `<Component><Prop>` (for example `BadgeSize { default = "default", small = "small" }`, `BadgeAnchorPosition { topLeft = "top-left", ... }`; use a camelCase member name when the value contains `-`). Member values match the Figma variant options and the DOM/theme values. Type the prop as ``BadgeSize | `${BadgeSize}` `` so JSX string values (`size="small"`) keep working, as ``background?: BackgroundColors | `${BackgroundColors}` `` does. Use the enum members, not raw strings, in implementations, `Record<BadgeSize, ...>` style maps, and tests. Existing models: `AlertStatus`, `TextSize`, `TitleColor`. Not covered: booleans, numbers, free strings, and token-name types derived from the theme (for example spacing or radius tokens). Before finishing, verify that no new `*.types.ts` declares a multi-value prop as a union type.
- Each React Native component **and each subcomponent that has styles** must own its own colocated `<name>.styles.native.ts` and import its own style hook. Never put subcomponent styles in the parent component's style file or have subcomponents source their styles from it. For example, `accordion.styles.native.ts` styles `Accordion` only, while `AccordionItem`, `AccordionHeader`, `AccordionBody`, and `AccordionIndicator` each use their own style file in their own folder. Keep `makeStyle`, theme tokens, state styling, and caller override precedence unchanged. A component with no styles needs no empty style file.
- For every new public component or subcomponent, add a colocated `docs.md` as the documentation site's source of truth. Include frontmatter fields `slug`, `name`, `family`, `familyOrder`, `order`, and `description`; optionally add `parent` for nested components. Write `## Examples` with `### Basic` first, followed by titled variations; put a concise description before every JSX code fence. Add `## API Reference` after the examples. Do not add separate Usage or Anatomy sections. The docs app renders examples directly from their Markdown fences, so keep each fence as a standalone JSX expression. The Next.js docs app discovers these files recursively and builds family navigation and routes from their metadata—do not maintain a separate component list or navigation registry. Reuse an existing family; introduce a new family only when the component does not fit an existing one, and assign a stable family order. Run `pnpm --filter @trilogy-ds/react check-docs` to verify every public barrel export has a colocated docs page.
- `CommonProps.style` is the shared styling escape hatch: Web accepts React `CSSProperties`, while Native accepts React Native `StyleProp<ViewStyle | TextStyle>`. Preserve each component's built-in styles and apply the caller's style last so consumer overrides take precedence. This generic passthrough does not define a named design variant and is not a Figma property.
- Load and follow [Trilogy Component JSDoc](../trilogy-component-jsdoc/SKILL.md) for every public component created or modified. It defines the shared template, required prop order (shared, Web, Native), and prop documentation rules.
- Prefer atomic composition when a component has distinct semantic regions that are reusable or whose content and order should be customizable. As with `Alert`, a container may accept `children` and expose `AlertContent`, `AlertTitle`, and `AlertDescription`. A `Box` with a header and footer may warrant `BoxHeader` and `BoxFooter` children.
- Do not artificially split simple standalone components such as `Title`, `Text`, or `Button`. Add only parts justified by the request; honor the explicit API and existing contracts. Use appropriate folders, exports, refs, and accessibility rules for public subcomponents without inventing functional behavior. For a new component, reuse functional conventions from comparable components only when needed.
- When using an existing component as a model, adapt names to the new component: types, interfaces, enums, variables, classes, files, exports, and Figma references. For `Text` modeled after `Title`, prefer `TextUiProps` and `TextLevel` over `TitleUiProps` and `TitleLevel`. Preserve prop names and values when they are requested unchanged, reuse generic types, and do not rename symbols in the source component.
